title: Screening: Use It for Asymptomatic Risk, Not Symptomatic Diagnosis
bottomLine: Screening is offered to asymptomatic people when evidence shows net benefit in a defined risk group. Symptoms move the patient into a diagnostic pathway, where screening intervals and eligibility rules no longer answer the clinical question.
recognize: Effective screening depends on disease burden, test performance, downstream treatment benefit and acceptable harms from false positives and overdiagnosis.
differentiate: Screening, surveillance after prior disease and diagnostic testing for symptoms are distinct pathways.
assessment: Before screening, confirm age/risk, prior test history, symptoms, life expectancy, patient values and whether follow-up treatment would be acceptable.
workup: Use current national evidence and provincial or territorial screening-program criteria; do not order a screening test outside its validated population simply because it exists.
management: Use shared decision-making when benefit-harm tradeoffs are preference-sensitive and ensure abnormal results reach diagnostic resolution.
medicationSafety: Not applicable; avoid preventive interventions whose treatment harms exceed expected screening benefit in severe frailty or limited life expectancy.
redFlags: Symptom being routed into screening rather than diagnosis
Screening continued despite no plausible benefit
counselling: Explain false positives, false negatives, overdiagnosis and absolute benefit in understandable terms.
followUp: Maintain a preventive-care registry or other reliable recall system.
examTrap: Ordering a screening mammogram for a new palpable breast mass and telling the patient to wait for the routine screening result.
oneLinePearl: Symptoms need diagnosis; screening is for people without the symptom.
sourceBasis: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care principles

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Program Test vs Diagnostic Colonoscopy
bottomLine: Average-risk asymptomatic adults use the current jurisdictional colorectal screening program, commonly stool-based testing at defined intervals. Rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss or significant bowel change requires diagnostic evaluation rather than routine screening.
recognize: Family history, hereditary syndrome and prior advanced polyps move patients out of average-risk screening pathways.
differentiate: A positive stool screening test requires colonoscopy; repeating the stool test is not an adequate substitute.
assessment: Confirm symptoms, family history, prior polyps/cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and last screening result.
workup: Follow the current provincial or territorial program for average risk and specialty surveillance for high-risk patients.
management: Arrange diagnostic colonoscopy after a positive screen and ensure pathology/follow-up is closed-loop.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural anticoagulant and diabetes-medication management must be individualized to the planned colonoscopy and possible polypectomy.
counselling: Explain that stool screening is effective for average-risk screening and does not need to be replaced by colonoscopy solely because colonoscopy feels more comprehensive.
followUp: Track completion after positive stool testing.
examTrap: Repeating a positive FIT to see if it becomes negative before referring for colonoscopy.
oneLinePearl: A positive colorectal screen is a diagnostic-colonoscopy problem.
sourceBasis: Provincial and territorial colorectal cancer screening programs

title: Breast Cancer Screening: Risk, Program, and Diagnostic Symptoms
bottomLine: Breast screening recommendations and program entry criteria differ across Canada and continue to evolve. Use the current local program and individual risk, but route a new mass, pathologic nipple discharge or inflammatory change into diagnostic imaging rather than routine screening.
recognize: High-risk genetic or family histories may warrant earlier MRI-based surveillance outside average-risk mammography programs.
differentiate: Screening mammography is for asymptomatic risk; diagnostic mammography/ultrasound evaluates symptoms.
assessment: Ask breast symptoms, family history, prior atypia/cancer, genetic risk, chest radiation and prior imaging.
workup: Use the current jurisdictional screening program for average risk and diagnostic breast imaging for symptoms; refer genetic-risk pathways when indicated.
management: Close the loop on abnormal imaging and biopsy recommendations and support shared decisions where the screening benefit-harm balance is preference-sensitive.
medicationSafety: Not applicable; hormone therapy decisions should consider individual breast-cancer risk without overstating absolute risk.
counselling: Explain that a recent normal screening mammogram does not rule out a new clinically important breast symptom.
followUp: Maintain risk-appropriate screening and diagnostic follow-through.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with a new breast mass because their screening mammogram six months ago was normal.
oneLinePearl: A new breast symptom outranks the old screening result.
sourceBasis: Provincial and territorial breast screening programs

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Low-Dose CT for Selected High-Risk People, Not Chest X-Ray
bottomLine: Lung cancer screening uses low-dose CT in eligible high-risk asymptomatic people through jurisdictional programs. Chest x-ray is not an effective lung cancer screening substitute, and symptoms such as hemoptysis or unexplained weight loss require diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Eligibility depends on age, smoking history and program-specific risk assessment, which varies across Canada.
differentiate: An incidental pulmonary nodule is a surveillance problem; a symptomatic suspicious lesion is a diagnostic oncology problem.
assessment: Assess current and former smoking, quit date, occupational exposures, symptoms, comorbidity and willingness to undergo follow-up/treatment.
workup: Refer eligible patients to the current provincial or territorial low-dose CT screening pathway.
management: Pair screening with smoking cessation support and ensure nodule follow-up is completed.
counselling: Explain false positives and incidental findings while emphasizing that screening does not replace smoking cessation.
followUp: Maintain program-defined repeat low-dose CT or diagnostic evaluation.
examTrap: Ordering an annual chest x-ray to screen a high-risk smoker for lung cancer.
oneLinePearl: Effective lung screening is low-dose CT in selected risk—not routine chest x-ray.

title: Prostate Cancer Screening: PSA Is a Preference-Sensitive Risk Test
bottomLine: PSA screening can reduce prostate cancer mortality for some patients but causes false positives, biopsy and overdiagnosis. Screening should be a shared decision based on age, ancestry/family risk, health status and preferences; urinary symptoms are evaluated diagnostically, not by screening logic alone.
recognize: Family history and some ancestry-related risk profiles increase prostate cancer risk.
differentiate: BPH elevates urinary symptoms and can raise PSA; prostatitis, ejaculation and recent instrumentation can also influence PSA.
assessment: Discuss values around early detection versus false positives and treatment harms; assess family history, life expectancy and prior PSA.
workup: Use current Canadian or provincial guidance for screening and repeat/adjunct testing before biopsy when appropriate.
management: Refer persistently concerning PSA or abnormal examination through urology pathways while avoiding screening in people unlikely to benefit.
medicationSafety: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA and change its interpretation.
counselling: Explain that PSA is prostate-specific, not cancer-specific.
followUp: Track repeat testing and referral rather than allowing a mildly abnormal PSA to disappear in the record.
examTrap: Ordering PSA automatically without discussing downstream biopsy and overdiagnosis tradeoffs in a patient where screening is preference-sensitive.
sourceBasis: Canadian urology and preventive screening guidance

title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening: Selected Risk, One-Time Imaging
bottomLine: AAA screening is a one-time ultrasound strategy for selected higher-risk asymptomatic adults under current Canadian guidance, not a universal repeated abdominal scan. New abdominal or back pain with hypotension is a diagnostic emergency regardless of screening history.
recognize: Smoking, older age, male sex and family history increase AAA risk.
differentiate: Screening a stable asymptomatic person is different from diagnosing suspected rupture or symptomatic aneurysm.
assessment: Review smoking and family history, vascular disease, age, health status and whether finding an aneurysm would alter management.
workup: Use abdominal ultrasound for screening; urgent CT/vascular imaging is used for symptomatic stable patients while unstable suspected rupture requires emergency vascular care.
management: Surveillance interval or repair referral depends on aneurysm size, growth and symptoms.
medicationSafety: Cardiovascular risk reduction includes smoking cessation, BP and lipid treatment; no medication reliably shrinks an AAA.
counselling: Explain that screening is intended to find aneurysms before rupture, when elective repair can be considered.
followUp: Ensure aneurysm surveillance is not lost between providers.
examTrap: Reassuring a hypotensive patient with sudden back pain because an ultrasound screening test three years ago was normal.
oneLinePearl: Past screening does not rule out today's aortic emergency.
sourceBasis: Canadian vascular and preventive care guidance

title: Type 2 Diabetes Screening: Risk, Glycemia, and Confirmation
bottomLine: Type 2 diabetes screening frequency depends on age and risk. Diagnostic thresholds require appropriate confirmation when the patient is asymptomatic and not in a hyperglycemic crisis; symptoms plus unequivocal hyperglycemia can establish diagnosis more directly.
recognize: Family history, gestational diabetes, cardiometabolic disease, obesity, medications and some population risks increase diabetes probability.
differentiate: Stress hyperglycemia during severe illness and corticosteroid therapy can be transient but still predict future diabetes risk.
assessment: Assess cardiometabolic risk, pregnancy history, medications, symptoms, food access and prior A1C/glucose trend.
workup: Use A1C, fasting glucose or oral glucose testing according to Diabetes Canada indications and limitations; A1C may be unreliable with altered red-cell turnover or some hemoglobinopathies.
management: Confirm diagnosis appropriately, begin lifestyle and pharmacologic management based on glycemia and cardiorenal risk, and screen complications at recommended intervals.
medicationSafety: Do not use A1C alone when a condition makes it analytically or biologically unreliable.
counselling: Use risk-based prevention counselling without blaming body size or culture.
followUp: Repeat screening at guideline-supported intervals when initial testing is normal.
examTrap: Diagnosing diabetes from one mildly elevated A1C in a patient with severe iron-deficiency anemia without confirming the result in context.
oneLinePearl: Choose the diabetes test the physiology can actually support.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada screening and diagnosis guidance

title: Cardiovascular Prevention: Treat Absolute Risk and Major Risk Conditions
bottomLine: Primary cardiovascular prevention integrates smoking, BP, lipids, diabetes, kidney disease, family history and absolute risk. Treat major risk conditions directly and use risk estimation to support shared statin and prevention decisions rather than treating one isolated number.
recognize: Established ASCVD, diabetes, CKD and very high lipid levels can justify treatment outside ordinary low-risk calculators.
differentiate: Primary prevention estimates future risk; secondary prevention applies after established atherosclerotic disease and generally warrants more intensive therapy.
assessment: Measure BP correctly, smoking/nicotine, lipids, glycemia, kidney function, family history, diet/activity, pregnancy potential and social access.
workup: Use current Canadian cardiovascular risk calculators and disease-specific guidance; avoid broad cardiac imaging in asymptomatic low-risk patients.
management: Address smoking, BP and lipids with evidence-based behavioural and pharmacologic therapy and cardiorenal risk reduction when diabetes/CKD is present.
medicationSafety: Statins are not routinely used during pregnancy; medication interactions and baseline liver or muscle disease may influence choice.
counselling: Discuss absolute expected benefit rather than presenting prevention as a pass/fail cholesterol target alone.
followUp: Reassess risk factors and adherence at clinically useful intervals.
examTrap: Ordering a stress test to screen an asymptomatic low-risk person instead of treating modifiable risk factors.
oneLinePearl: Prevent future events by treating risk, not by searching asymptomatic arteries for disease without indication.

title: Sexual Health Screening: Ask Practices, Not Identity Labels
bottomLine: STI and HIV screening should be normalized and based on age, pregnancy, exposures, new partners, local epidemiology and patient preference. Ask about sexual practices and anatomic sites rather than inferring risk from orientation, gender or relationship status.
recognize: Asymptomatic infection is common, especially chlamydia, gonorrhea at extragenital sites, syphilis and early HIV.
differentiate: Screening is preventive; symptoms such as pelvic pain, ulcers or discharge require diagnostic testing and treatment pathways.
assessment: Use the five-P style domains—partners, practices, protection, past STIs and pregnancy intentions—adapted respectfully to the patient.
workup: Use current PHAC site-specific NAAT and serology guidance and include pregnancy-specific screening.
management: Offer vaccines, PrEP/PEP, contraception and treatment/partner management as indicated.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy and allergies change some STI treatment choices.
counselling: Normalize routine screening so testing is not framed as suspicion or accusation.
followUp: Use retesting and test-of-cure intervals from current PHAC guidance.
examTrap: Skipping STI screening because a patient describes their relationship as monogamous without asking about risk or preference.
oneLinePearl: Sexual risk lives in exposures, not labels.

title: Bone Health Screening: Fracture Risk Before the First Fracture
bottomLine: Bone-health screening uses age, sex, prior fracture, glucocorticoids, falls and secondary osteoporosis risk to decide when DXA and fracture-risk assessment are appropriate. A prior low-trauma hip or vertebral fracture already signals high risk even without a screening DXA.
recognize: Loss of height, kyphosis and prior fragility fracture are important clues.
differentiate: Screening before fracture differs from diagnostic evaluation after a fracture or concerning bone pain.
assessment: Review fracture/fall history, menopause/hypogonadism, steroids, smoking, alcohol, nutrition, CKD and malabsorption.
workup: Use DXA and Canadian fracture-risk tools when indicated and evaluate secondary causes selectively.
management: Use exercise/fall prevention and pharmacotherapy based on absolute fracture risk and prior fracture history.
medicationSafety: Denosumab requires an exit/transition plan; bisphosphonates have renal and GI considerations.
counselling: Explain that bone medication benefit is fracture prevention, not an immediate pain effect.
followUp: Avoid repeating DXA more often than needed to change management.
examTrap: Withholding osteoporosis treatment after a fragility hip fracture because a DXA has not yet been performed.
oneLinePearl: A fragility fracture can establish treatment-level risk before DXA does.

title: Adult Vaccine Review: Risk Changes After Childhood
bottomLine: Adult immunization is not just childhood catch-up. Pregnancy, age, chronic disease, occupation, travel, asplenia and immunocompromise create new indications for influenza, COVID-19, pertussis, pneumococcal, zoster, RSV and other vaccines under current NACI guidance.
recognize: Vaccine recommendations and publicly funded eligibility can differ and change rapidly.
differentiate: National NACI recommendation is clinical evidence guidance; provincial or territorial funding determines access in many settings.
assessment: Review current products/doses, pregnancy, immune status, asplenia, chronic lung/heart/renal disease, travel and occupation.
workup: Do not order routine serology for every vaccine; use it only where current guidance supports it.
management: Offer indicated vaccines and co-administer compatible products when appropriate; use the 2026 Canadian Immunization Guide as the clinical reference and verify local product/funding rules.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines and timing around immunosuppressive therapy require special review.
counselling: Address vaccine concerns with evidence and avoid implying that lack of funding means lack of clinical indication.
followUp: Document series completion and next dose dates.
examTrap: Assuming a fully immunized 30-year-old never needs vaccine review again until age 65.
oneLinePearl: Adult vaccine risk changes with life stage and disease.

title: Preventive Visit Prioritization: Do the High-Value Work First
bottomLine: A preventive visit should prioritize interventions that meaningfully reduce morbidity and mortality—tobacco treatment, BP, immunization, indicated cancer screening, cardiometabolic risk, mental health and social needs—rather than low-value blanket testing.
recognize: Routine annual ECGs, chest x-rays, broad lab panels and imaging in asymptomatic low-risk adults often create false positives without proven benefit.
differentiate: Periodic preventive care can be delivered opportunistically across visits and does not require a ritual annual battery of tests.
assessment: Use age/risk, prior screening, family history, immunization, medications, mental health, substance use, sexual health and social determinants to build priorities.
workup: Order tests only when a guideline or individual risk creates a reasonable chance of benefit.
management: Use reminders, standing orders and team-based preventive workflows so high-value care is not crowded out by low-value tests.
medicationSafety: Preventive polypharmacy should be reconsidered when expected time-to-benefit exceeds life expectancy or treatment burden conflicts with goals.
redFlags: Symptom hidden inside a preventive visit
Preventive plan impossible because of access barriers
counselling: Explain why more testing is not always better medicine.
followUp: Create a prioritized plan for preventive items that cannot all be completed in one visit.
examTrap: Ordering a routine annual ECG, chest x-ray and large laboratory panel for an asymptomatic low-risk adult instead of addressing smoking and hypertension.
oneLinePearl: High-value prevention is targeted, not maximal testing.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada primary care recommendations
